segments.translit: prajñāpāramitārthāmṛtapānaparituṣṭā hi kukkuripādāḥ | tam evārtham ātmani bhagavatīnairātmāyoginīm adhimucya vadanti —
segments.translation: [Kukkurīpāda]{p-kukkuri} is fully contented by drinking the [nectar]{amrta} of the meaning of the [perfection of wisdom]{prajnaparamita}. Setting his [resolve]{adhimukti}, in himself, on that very meaning, the [Blessed Lady]{p-bhagavati}, the [Nairātmā]{nairatma} [yoginī]{yogini}, he speaks:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song: Kukkurīpāda, sated with the nectar of the [perfection of wisdom]{prajnaparamita}, has resolved on himself as that very meaning, the Blessed Lady [Nairātmā]{nairatma} ('she who is without self'), and so speaks (cp.20.m1). The Tibetan instead has him devoted to the goddess as the embodiment of reality, without 'in himself'.

flags.note: Munidatta's Sanskrit (cp.20.m1) has tam evārtham ātmani ... adhimucya, 'setting his resolve, in himself, on that very meaning', that is, taking himself to be the goddess. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has de kho na nyid kyi don gyi bdag nyid bcom ldan 'das ma bdag med ma'i rnal 'byor ma la lhag par mos nas, 'devoted to the Blessed Lady Nairātmā yoginī, whose nature is the meaning of reality': as if reading tattvārtha for tam evārtham and taking ātman as 'nature, embodiment' instead of 'in himself'. It loses the self-identification. I follow the Sanskrit.

Shastri prints bhagavatī nairātmāyoginīm with a space; I read one compound, bhagavatīnairātmāyoginīm, which removes the apparent mismatch of a nominative beside an accusative. The honorific plural kukkuripādāḥ ... vadanti is rendered in the singular.

segments.translit:
hām̐u nirāsī ityādi | ahaṃ bhagavatī nairātmā nirāsā | āsaṅgarahitā | khamaṇa iti sarvaśūnyaṃ manaḥsvāmī | asya su[ra]tābhiṣvaṅgeṇa mama viśiṣṭasaṃyogākṣarasukhānubhava[ḥ] kasminn api kathāvedyo na bhavatīti |
tathā ca sarahapādāḥ —
ko pattijjai kasu kahami ajja kattāi a āu
piyadaṃśaṇe hale ṇa ṭvalesi saṃsāsaṣuṛa jāu ||
segments.translation:
'I am without desire…' and so on. I, the [Blessed Lady]{p-bhagavati} [Nairātmā]{nairatma}, am without desire (nirāsā), that is, free of attachment. '[Khamaṇa]{khamana}': the wholly empty mind is the lord. Through attachment to [lovemaking]{surata} with him, my experience of the [imperishable bliss]{aksara-sukha} of distinguished union cannot in any way be known through speech.
And so [Saraha]{p-saraha} says:
Who would believe it? To whom can I tell it? Today the beloved came.
At the sight of the beloved, friend, I did not waver; let mother-in-law and father-in-law go.
segments.note: Munidatta hears the Blessed Lady [Nairātmā]{nairatma} speaking: she is free of attachment, and her husband, [khamaṇa]{khamana}, is the wholly empty mind. Through attachment to lovemaking with him, her experience of imperishable bliss in distinguished union cannot be known through words; Saraha's verse asks who would believe it (cp.20.m2). The Tibetan makes the husband 'the lord of the mind'.

equations.en: the wholly empty mind (sarvaśūnyaṃ manaḥ), as the lord (svāmin)

citations.quoted: ko pattijjai kasu kahami ajja kattāi a āu / piyadaṃśaṇe hale ṇa ṭvalesi saṃsāsaṣuṛa jāu
citations.work: Saraha, as Munidatta names him; the work is not named (perhaps one of his dohā collections)

flags.note: khamaṇa iti sarvaśūnyaṃ manaḥsvāmī (cp.20.m2): a neuter adjective beside a masculine compound. I take it as kha = 'empty', maṇa = 'mind', and svāmin glossing the song's bhatāra: 'the wholly empty mind is the lord'. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads nam mkha'i yid can ... thams cad stong pa la yid kyi bdag po, 'having a sky-mind ... the lord of the mind, in the all-empty', taking manaḥsvāmī as 'lord of the mind'.

su[ra]tābhiṣvaṅgeṇa: the syllable ra is Shastri's restoration. The Tibetan has shin du bde ba la mngon par chags pas, 'through attachment to exceeding bliss', which fits surata rendered by its parts (su- = shin du) but could also reflect another word, such as sukha.

For viśiṣṭasaṃyoga, 'distinguished union', the Tibetan has khyad par du 'phags pa yang dag pa'i sbyor ba, 'distinguished, perfect union', apparently reading saṃyoga as samyag-yoga. The sense is not affected.

The Tibetan parallel of this segment ends with the prose (gang du yang smra ru yod pa ma yin pa'o) and has nothing for the verse Munidatta quotes from Saraha (cp.20.m2), so the verse cannot be checked against it.

Saraha's Apabhraṃśa verse is corrupt and my rendering of it is partly conjectural. Clear: ko pattijjai, 'who would believe it?'; kasu kahami, 'to whom can I tell it?'; piyadaṃśaṇe, 'at the sight of the beloved'; hale, vocative to a woman friend. Guesses: (1) ajja kattāi a āu taken as 'today the beloved (kanta?) came'; (2) ṇa ṭvalesi taken as ṇa ṭalesi, 'did not waver', a past in -esi like the song's own bhailesi (4a); it may instead be a second person, 'you do not turn aside'; (3) saṃsāsaṣuṛa jāu taken as sāsu sasura, 'mother-in-law and father-in-law' (Munidatta cites the father-in-law of song 2 as sasurā), with jāu 'let go'; it may instead hide saṃsāra, 'saṃsāra goes'. Only the first line is needed for Munidatta's point (cp.20.m2), that the experience cannot be told.

kasminn api kathāvedyo na bhavati: I take the locative as 'in any way at all'; it could also mean 'to anyone at all'. The Tibetan gang du yang smra ru yod pa ma yin pa, 'there is no way to speak of it anywhere', supports the first. His paraphrase puts 'my experience of imperishable bliss' where the song has mohora bigoā, without an explicit gloss; the Tibetan line of 1b has nyams myong, 'experience'.

segments.translit:
dhrupadena tam evārthaṃ draḍhayanti —
phiṭalesv ityādi | ata evāntam iti paryantaḥ | mahāsukhacakrasvakuṭīṃ dṛṣṭvā sphuṭam iti | viṣayādivṛndaṃ mayā nairātmayā tasmin samaye niṣkṛntitaṃ | svayam evātmānaṃ sambodhya vadati | bho mātar nairātme | tad idānī[ṃ] yaṃ yaṃ viṣayāriṃ paśyāmy atra sa ko 'pi na vidyate | sarveṣā[ṃ] mahāsukhamayatvāt |
segments.translation: With the [refrain]{dhruvapada} he makes that same meaning firm: 'I broke away' and so on. Hence 'end' means the limit. Having seen my own [hut]{hut}, the [wheel of great bliss]{mahasukha-cakra}: 'burst' (sphuṭa). The host of [sense objects]{visaya} and the rest was cut off by me, [Nairātmā]{nairatma}, at that moment. She speaks, addressing her very self: 'O [mother]{mother}, Nairātmā! So now, whatever enemy among the sense objects I see here, not one of them exists, for all are made of [great bliss]{mahasukha}.'
segments.note: Munidatta reads the refrain as [Nairātmā]{nairatma} speaking: at the end, the limit, she has seen her own hut, the [wheel of great bliss]{mahasukha-cakra}, and at that moment has cut off the host of sense objects. Calling herself 'mother, Nairātmā', she says that no enemy she sees among the sense objects exists, since all are made of great bliss (cp.20.m3).

equations.src: phiṭalesu (the song has pheṭaliu), as sphuṭa

flags.note: mahāsukhacakrasvakuṭīṃ dṛṣṭvā sphuṭam iti (cp.20.m3): I take sphuṭa as Munidatta's Sanskrit for the song's pheṭaliu ('I broke away'; the root sphuṭ-, 'burst, split'), explained by the next sentence, the cutting off of the sense objects. It could instead be an adverb with dṛṣṭvā, 'having clearly seen'. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has bltas nas 'phro ba'o, 'having looked, it radiates', a third sense.

Munidatta's paraphrase of 2b, yaṃ yaṃ viṣayāriṃ paśyāmy atra sa ko 'pi na vidyate (cp.20.m3), has 'I see' where the song has bāhāma (draft: 'carried'). The Tibetan line has 'bab pa, 'falls, flows down'. I translate his wording and do not harmonize it with the song.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) cites the refrain as spangs nas, 'having abandoned', as its line does (its line also has kye'i mi, 'O man', where the Bengali has go māe, 'O mother'); it makes mtha' ma, 'the end', 'the ultimate' (mthar thug pa'i) house of the wheel of great bliss, without 'own'; it has bdag gis bdag med pa, 'by me, the selfless', not the goddess's name bdag med ma; and sel ba, 'clear away', for niṣkṛntita, 'cut off'. It then breaks off mid-sentence and resumes with the close of the comment on couplet 4 (cp.20.m5), so the address to the mother and what follows have no Tibetan.

vadati carries no gender. I write 'she' because the speaker has just been named mayā nairātmayā, 'by me, Nairātmā'; in cp.20.m5 the same formula has a masculine vocative (kāyavajra). mahāsukhacakrasvakuṭī is taken as 'my own hut, the wheel of great bliss'; it could be 'my own hut in the wheel of great bliss'. viṣayāri, 'the enemy that is the sense objects', recurs in cp.20.m6.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadena vicārasvarūpam āha —
pahile ityādi | ādau saṃvṛtivāsanāpuṭaṃ kāyo 'yaṃ prasūtaḥ [prasūtaṃ] | asya kāyasya nāḍī dvātriṃśaddevī tasya piṇḍīkramānupūrvyā sadguruvacanapramāṇato vicāryamāṇe sati saiva vāsanā varākī kathaṃ vidyate | na vidyate eva paraṃ |
segments.translation: With the second [verse]{pada} he states the [true nature]{svarupa} of [examination]{vicara}: 'At first…' and so on. At first this [body]{body} was born, a casket of [conventional]{samvrti} [habitual tendencies]{vasana}. The [channels]{nadi} of this body are the thirty-two goddesses. When it is examined in the order of the [piṇḍīkrama]{pindikrama}, on the authority of the words of the true [guru]{guru}, how could that same [poor wretch]{bapura}, the habitual tendencies, be found? It is simply not found at all.
segments.note: Munidatta calls this verse the nature of examination. The body was born at first as a casket of conventional [habitual tendencies]{vasana}; its channels are the thirty-two goddesses. When it is examined in the order of the [piṇḍīkrama]{pindikrama}, the 'condensed sequence', on the true guru's authority, that 'poor wretch', the tendencies, is not found at all (cp.20.m4).

equations.en: a casket of conventional habitual tendencies (saṃvṛtivāsanāpuṭa), which the body was born as
that same vāsanā, the habitual tendencies

flags.note: No Tibetan for this segment: the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) passes from the comment on the refrain straight into the end of the comment on couplet 4, so Munidatta's Sanskrit here (cp.20.m4) cannot be checked. The Tibetan line of 3a has rnam shes, 'consciousness', where his paraphrase has the body born (kāyo 'yaṃ prasūtaḥ); no Tibetan comment survives to show how its translators read this.

prasūtaḥ[taṃ]: Shastri's bracket offers prasūtaṃ, agreeing with puṭaṃ. With prasūtaḥ, 'this body was born as a casket of tendencies'; with prasūtaṃ, 'a casket of tendencies was produced: this body'. The sense barely changes.

asya kāyasya nāḍī dvātriṃśaddevī tasya ... vicāryamāṇe sati: nāḍī is formally singular, and dvātriṃśaddevī may be a collective, 'the group of thirty-two goddesses'; tasya ... vicāryamāṇe sati mixes a genitive with a locative absolute. I take the thing examined to be the body.
Munidatta cites the couplet as pahile, 'at first' (cp.20.m4), where Shastri's song has pahila, 'first'; his ādau, 'at first', follows his own form, so the quotation is rendered 'At first…'.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena abhyāsaphalam āha —
navayauvanetyādi | mūlaṃ saṃvṛtibodhicittaṃ | tasya nikṛttiḥ | maṇimūle maṇyantargate mayā nairātmabhāvakena kukkuripādena kṛtā |
tathā ca śrīhevajre —
tīradvayaṃ bhaved ghaṇṭāṃ |
sa tena hetunā viṣayamaṇḍalopasaṃhārakṛtaṃ navayauvanam iti | tatprabhāvāt dvātriṃśallakṣaṇavyañjanāśītimahāvajradharaśarīrasundaro bhūto 'si bhoḥ kāyavajra sādhum etat | svayam ātmānaṃ sambodhya vadatīti |
segments.translation:
With the third [verse]{pada} he states the fruit of [practice]{abhyasa}: 'Fresh youth…' and so on. The [root]{root} is [conventional]{samvrti} [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}. Its cutting was done at the [root of the jewel]{manimula}, within the jewel, by me, [Kukkurīpāda]{p-kukkuri}, meditating on [selflessness]{nairatmya}.
And so in the glorious [Hevajra]{tx-hevajra}:
The pair of banks would be the [bell]{bell}.
For that reason, 'fresh youth' is youth made by the withdrawal of the [maṇḍala]{mandala} of [sense objects]{visaya}. By its power you have become beautiful with the body of the great [Vajradhara]{p-vajradhara}, with the [thirty-two marks and eighty signs]{laksana-vyanjana}, O body-vajra: this is excellent. He speaks addressing himself.
segments.note: Munidatta calls this verse the fruit of practice. The root is conventional [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, which Kukkurīpāda, meditating on selflessness, cut at the root of the jewel. He cites the line as 'fresh youth', made by withdrawing the [maṇḍala]{mandala} of sense objects; by its power he, addressing himself as 'body-vajra', has become beautiful with Vajradhara's body (cp.20.m5).

equations.en: youth made by the withdrawal of the maṇḍala of sense objects

citations.work: Hevajra Tantra (Munidatta names it as the Śrī Hevajra; I cannot place the line)

flags.note: Munidatta cites the couplet as navayauvana, 'fresh youth' (cp.20.m5), where Shastri's song has jāṇa jaubaṇa (draft: 'Know: my youth'). The Tibetan line has bdag ni gzhon nu dar ma rdzogs par gyur, 'my youthful prime became complete', with no 'know'. His text may have read ṇava (nava), 'fresh', where Shastri prints jāṇa.

The Hevajra line tīradvayaṃ bhaved ghaṇṭāṃ has an accusative, ghaṇṭām, where a nominative is expected, and reads like a fragment of a longer verse. I translate 'the pair of banks would be the bell', but I cannot place the line or say how Munidatta means it to bear on the cutting at the root of the jewel (cp.20.m5). The Tibetan does not cover it.

sa tena hetunā: the masculine sa has nothing to agree with (perhaps for sā, 'that cutting', or a stray syllable); I render 'For that reason'. maṇimūle maṇyantargate: taken as 'at the root of the jewel, within the jewel'; it could be a locative absolute, 'when it had gone inside the jewel'.

nairātmabhāvakena: 'meditating on selflessness' (nairātmya), as the glossary has it; it could also be 'meditating on Nairātmā', the goddess. Here the speaker is 'me, Kukkurīpāda', masculine, where in cp.20.m2 and cp.20.m3 the 'I' was Nairātmā. For upasaṃhāra I write 'withdrawal', not the glossary's 'summing up', and leave it unmarked (see questions).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) covers only the end of this segment, from tatprabhāvāt (de'i mthu las). It has rdo rje 'dzin pa chen po'i gnas la sku mdzes par gyur, 'the body became beautiful in the state of the great Vajradhara', adding gnas, 'state', and it has khyod kye'i sku rdo rje lags so, 'you, O body-vajra, are so', where the Sanskrit has sādhum etat, 'this is excellent'. The sense is close.
Munidatta's comment (cp.20.m5) says nothing about the father destroyed (bāpa saṃghārā) in 4b; the Tibetan line has no father either.

segments.translit:
caturthapadena sākṣātkāritvam āha —
bhaṇathītyādi | eṣa saṃvṛtibodhicitto hi bhavaḥ | sthiram iti sthiraṃ kṛtvā prajñāravindair dhairyair yogīndrair nirañjanarūpeṇāvagata[ṃ] te 'smin bhavamaṇḍale viṣayārimardanāt vīrāḥ |
tathā kṛṣṇācāryapādāḥ —
jem̐ bujhia avirala sahaja kṣaṇu ityādi || 20 ||
segments.translation:
With the fourth [verse]{pada} he states [direct realization]{saksatkara}: 'Says…' and so on. For this [existence]{bhava} is [conventional]{samvrti} [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}. 'Steady' means: having made it [steady]{sthira}, it is understood in the form of [the stainless]{niranjana} by steadfast [lords of yogis]{yogindra} who have the [lotus]{lotus} of [wisdom]{prajna}. They are [heroes]{vira} in this [maṇḍala]{mandala} of existence, because they crush the enemy, the [sense objects]{visaya}.
And so [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha}:
Whoever has understood the uninterrupted [innate]{sahaja} moment…
and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta calls the last verse direct realization. Existence here is conventional bodhicitta; made steady, it is understood as [the stainless]{niranjana} by steadfast lords of yogis with the lotus of wisdom. Crushing the enemy, the sense objects, they are heroes in this maṇḍala of existence. He adds Kṛṣṇācārya's line on understanding the uninterrupted innate moment (cp.20.m6).

equations.en: heroes, because they crush the enemy, the sense objects, in this maṇḍala of existence

citations.work: Kṛṣṇācārya (Kāṇha), as Munidatta names him; probably his Dohākoṣa

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) differs in detail from Munidatta's Sanskrit (cp.20.m6): 'dir, 'here', for eṣa, 'this'; shes rab kyi chu skyes la, 'in the lotus of wisdom', a locative, for the instrumental prajñāravindaiḥ; no word for dhairyaiḥ, 'steadfast'; dmigs pa med pa'i ngo bos, 'in the nature of non-apprehension (without object)', for nirañjanarūpeṇa, 'in the form of the stainless'; and a relative construction, 'whichever lords of yogis understood it, those...'. In Kāṇha's line it has skad cig gis, 'in an instant', where the Apabhraṃśa makes the moment what is understood.

prajñāravindaiḥ: taken as a possessive compound with yogīndraiḥ, 'who have the lotus of wisdom'; it could also be instrumental of means, 'through lotuses of wisdom'. The sentence has te, 'they', with no relative to pick up; avagata[ṃ] has Shastri's restored anusvāra.
Shastri prints dhairyyer (ধৈর্য্যের্), not a Sanskrit form; I read dhairyair, 'steadfast', agreeing with yogīndraiḥ. The Tibetan has no word for it.

Munidatta names the author of the quoted line Kṛṣṇācārya (cp.20.m6); I keep that name form as the surface of {p-kanha}, whose entry gives 'Kāṇha'. Only the opening words of the verse are quoted: jem̐ bujhia, 'by whom (it is) understood'.

questions: 4a: Munidatta cites the line as navayauvana, 'fresh youth' (cp.20.m5), and the Tibetan line (bdag ni gzhon nu dar ma rdzogs par gyur) has no 'know'. Both point to a text with ṇava or nava where Shastri prints jāṇa. Should the draft's 'Know:' be flagged, or the line emended?

1a: both Munidatta (nirāsā, glossed āsaṅgarahitā, 'free of attachment', cp.20.m2) and the Tibetan line (chags med) take nirāsī as 'without attachment'. The draft has 'without desire', and I kept that wording where he quotes the line. Should the draft move to 'without attachment'?

2b: Munidatta paraphrases with 'whatever enemy among the sense objects I see here' (cp.20.m3), so he has 'see' where the song has bāhāma (draft: 'carried'), and the Tibetan line has 'bab pa, 'falls, flows down'. Does the draft's 'carried' need a flag?

cp.20.m3: I took sphuṭa as Munidatta's Sanskrit for the song's pheṭaliu, 'burst, broke away', explained by the cutting off of the sense objects. It might instead be 'clearly' (with 'having seen'), and the Tibetan has 'phro ba, 'radiates'. Which reading do you prefer?

The glossary entry upasamhara gives 'summing up', which fits song 15 but not viṣayamaṇḍalopasaṃhāra in cp.20.m5, where Munidatta means the withdrawal of the sense objects. I wrote 'withdrawal' and left it unmarked. Should the entry take 'withdrawal' as a variant, or be split?

Saraha's verse in cp.20.m2 is corrupt, and my second line (the in-laws, 'did not waver') is conjecture. Could it be checked against an edition of Saraha's dohās? Similarly, can the Hevajra fragment tīradvayaṃ bhaved ghaṇṭāṃ (cp.20.m5) be located, and is it a twilight-language code?

The speaker changes: Kukkurīpāda resolves on himself as Nairātmā (cp.20.m1), the 'I' of cp.20.m2 and cp.20.m3 is Nairātmā (feminine), and in cp.20.m5 it is 'me, Kukkurīpāda', addressed as 'body-vajra' (masculine). I wrote 'she' for the ungendered vadati of cp.20.m3. Is that acceptable?
In cp.20.m6 I wrote [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha} to keep Munidatta's name form; the entry's English is 'Kāṇha'. Which should commentary translations use?
